questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The electorate Article One points to for House votes
questions.learningObjective: Identify the electorate Article One points to for House votes

All adult citizens regardless of state law
options.misconception: ignores the state-reference in Article One

options.text: Only property-owning freeholders
Voters qualified for the United States Senate

questions.explanation: Article One, Section 2 ties House voter qualifications to those for the state legislature's larger house. It does not impose a uniform federal standard.

questions.topic: The three qualifications for a Representative
questions.learningObjective: List the three qualifications for a Representative
questions.stem: A bar graph of constitutional qualifications asks for a Representative's three; which set is correct?

options.text: Age thirty, nine years a citizen, and an inhabitant of the state
options.misconception: uses Senate qualifications for the House

options.text: Age twenty-five, seven years a citizen, and an inhabitant of the state
Age thirty-five, fourteen years a citizen, and a natural-born citizen
Age eighteen, five years a citizen, and a resident of the district
options.misconception: lowers the thresholds and adds a district rule

questions.explanation: A Representative must be at least twenty-five, a citizen for seven years, and an inhabitant of the state. The other sets describe the Senate or Presidency.
questions.hint: Twenty-five, seven years, state inhabitant.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The gap between the two sets of qualifications
questions.learningObjective: Explain the gap between House and Senate qualifications
questions.stem: A student explains the difference between House and Senate qualifications; give a model answer.

answer.exemplar: The Senate requires age thirty and nine years of citizenship, while the House requires age twenty-five and seven years, so the Senate demands greater age and longer citizenship.

questions.explanation: The Senate's thresholds are higher in both age and citizenship years. The gap reflects the chamber's longer terms and smaller size.
questions.hint: Senate needs thirty years and nine years of citizenship.

options.text: inhabitant of that state
options.misconception: the phrase is shared, not differing

options.text: citizen of the United States
options.misconception: shared language, not the differing phrase

options.text: when elected
qualified elector
options.misconception: not the phrase used in either clause

questions.explanation: The phrase when elected appears in the Senate clause but not the House clause, marking the timing difference. The other phrases are shared or absent.
questions.hint: The Senate clause adds when elected.

options.text: Only property owners
All persons equally
options.misconception: ignores the three-fifths and Indian exclusions

options.text: Only free white male citizens
Free persons including servants, excluding Indians not taxed, plus three-fifths of other persons

questions.explanation: The original apportionment counted free persons including servants, excluded Indians not taxed, and added three-fifths of other persons. Equal counting came later.
questions.hint: Free persons, untaxed Indians excluded, three-fifths of others.

questions.stem: A table shows 10000 other persons in a state; under the original rule, how many are added to the apportionment count?
questions.explanation: Three-fifths of 10000 is 6000. Using the full count or one-fifth would be wrong.
questions.hint: Multiply by three-fifths.

options.text: One Representative per 100000 persons
One Representative per 50000 persons
One Representative per 30000 persons
No more than one per 10000 persons

questions.explanation: Article One, Section 2 sets one Representative per 30000 persons as the cap. Larger ratios came later by statute.

options.text: Two hundred and eighteen Representatives
One hundred and five Representatives
Forty-one Representatives
Sixty-five Representatives

questions.explanation: The original allotment fixed sixty-five Representatives among the thirteen states until the first enumeration. Later apportionments changed the number.
questions.hint: The original allotment was sixty-five.

questions.topic: How often the enumeration must be taken
questions.learningObjective: State how often the enumeration must be taken

options.text: Every five years
Every ten years
Every twenty years
Only once, after ratification
options.misconception: treats the first enumeration as the only one

questions.explanation: The enumeration must be made within every subsequent term of ten years. A one-time or other interval misstates the rule.
questions.hint: The interval is ten years.

questions.topic: Who issues a writ for a House vacancy
questions.learningObjective: Identify who issues a writ for a House vacancy
questions.stem: A vacancy procedure graph asks who issues the writ for a House vacancy; what is correct?

options.text: The President of the United States
options.misconception: assigns the duty to the executive branch

options.text: The Speaker of the House
options.misconception: confuses House internal authority with state authority

options.text: The governor of the state
The Supreme Court
options.misconception: assigns the duty to the judiciary

questions.explanation: The executive authority of the state issues writs of election to fill House vacancies. The Speaker, President, and Court do not.
questions.hint: The state's executive authority issues the writ.

options.text: A fractional vote shared with the other senator
Two votes, one for each class
A vote weighted by state population
options.misconception: imports House apportionment into the Senate

options.text: One vote

questions.explanation: Each senator has one vote. Classes and population do not alter the equal vote.
questions.hint: Each senator casts one vote.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Dividing the Senate into three classes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of dividing the Senate into three classes
questions.stem: A student explains why the Senate is divided into three classes; give a model answer.

answer.exemplar: The three classes ensure that roughly one-third of senators face election every two years, so the Senate is never entirely replaced at once and continuity is preserved.

questions.explanation: Staggered classes keep two-thirds of the Senate in place each election. Electing all at once would break continuity.
questions.hint: One-third is elected every two years.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The temporary appointment sentence in Section 3
questions.learningObjective: Identify the temporary appointment provision in Section 3
questions.stem: A vacancy graph asks about the temporary appointment sentence in Section 3; what does it allow?

options.text: The Senate appoints a replacement for the full term
options.misconception: confuses vacancy with internal Senate power

options.text: The governor may make temporary appointments until the next election
The President appoints a replacement without confirmation
options.misconception: assigns the power to the executive branch

options.text: No temporary appointment is ever allowed

questions.explanation: Section 3 lets the state executive make temporary appointments until the next election, as the state legislature provides. The Senate and President do not fill the seat.
questions.hint: The governor may make temporary appointments.

questions.stem: A leadership graph shows the Vice President's Senate role; what is it?

options.text: Presiding officer with no vote at all
Voting member with equal status to other senators
options.misconception: overstates the Vice President's voting power

options.text: President of the Senate with a tie-breaking vote
Chair of the majority party caucus

questions.explanation: The Vice President is President of the Senate and votes only to break ties. The role is not a full voting membership.
questions.hint: President of the Senate, tie-breaker only.

questions.topic: The two occasions for a President pro tempore
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two occasions for a President pro tempore
questions.stem: A Senate procedure graph asks when a President pro tempore presides; which two occasions?

options.text: When a quorum is absent or present
When the Senate is in recess or in session
When the President is impeached or removed
When the Vice President is absent or when exercising the Vice President's office

questions.explanation: The President pro tempore presides when the Vice President is absent, and serves when the Vice President exercises the office of President. Recess and quorum are not triggers.
questions.hint: Vice President absent or exercising the presidency.

questions.topic: Who presides over a presidential trial
questions.learningObjective: Identify who presides over a presidential impeachment trial
questions.stem: An impeachment trial graph asks who presides when the President is tried; what is correct?

options.text: The Vice President
options.misconception: the Vice President presides over other trials

options.text: The Chief Justice of the United States
The President pro tempore
The Speaker of the House

questions.explanation: The Chief Justice presides over a presidential impeachment trial. The Vice President and President pro tempore preside over other trials.
questions.hint: The Chief Justice presides over presidential trials.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two-thirds that convicts
questions.learningObjective: State the vote required to convict on impeachment
questions.stem: An impeachment outcome graph asks what vote convicts; what is required?

options.text: A three-fourths vote of all senators
options.misconception: raises the threshold and changes the base

options.text: A simple majority of members present
A two-thirds vote of members present
A unanimous vote of the Senate

questions.explanation: Conviction requires a two-thirds vote of the members present. A simple majority suffices only for House impeachment, not Senate conviction.
questions.hint: Two-thirds of members present convicts.

questions.topic: What a judgment on impeachment may reach
questions.learningObjective: State what an impeachment judgment may reach
questions.stem: A sanctions graph asks what an impeachment judgment may include; what is correct?

options.text: Civil fines and restitution
options.misconception: imports civil remedies not in the clause

options.text: Removal and criminal penalties
options.misconception: adds criminal penalties the clause excludes

options.text: Only censure, not removal
Removal from office and disqualification from future office

questions.explanation: An impeachment judgment may reach removal and disqualification from future federal office. Criminal penalties are left to ordinary courts.
questions.hint: Removal and disqualification only.

options.text: Times, qualifications, and manner of voters
Times, places, and manner of holding elections
Places, manner, and results of elections
options.misconception: adds results, not in the clause

options.text: Times, places, and winners of elections
options.misconception: adds winners, not in the clause

questions.explanation: The Elections Clause covers times, places, and manner of holding elections for Senators and Representatives. Qualifications and results are not included.
questions.hint: Times, places, and manner.

questions.stem: An elections power graph asks what Congress may not alter; what is correct?

options.text: The places where elections are held
The manner of holding elections
The times of choosing Senators
The qualifications of voters
options.misconception: Congress generally may not alter voter qualifications, but the clause specifically protects the times of choosing Senators

questions.explanation: The Elections Clause lets Congress alter times, places, and manner except the times of choosing Senators. The proviso protects senatorial election timing.
questions.hint: Congress may not alter the times of choosing Senators.

questions.stem: An elections clause graph asks how Congress exercises its power to alter; what is the form?

options.text: By constitutional amendment
By resolution of one House
By executive order
options.misconception: assigns the power to the President

options.text: By law

questions.explanation: Congress exercises its Elections Clause power by law. A single-House resolution or executive order would not suffice.

questions.stem: An elections authority graph asks who makes the default rules; what is correct?

options.text: Congress exclusively
The legislature of each state
The governor of each state
options.misconception: assigns the default to the executive

options.text: The federal courts
options.misconception: assigns the default to the judiciary

questions.explanation: The state legislature is the default rulemaker under the Elections Clause; Congress may override by law. The governor and courts do not set the default.
questions.hint: State legislatures set the default rules.

questions.topic: Each House as the judge of its own members

options.text: The President
options.misconception: assigns the power to the executive

options.text: The Supreme Court
options.misconception: assigns the power to the judiciary

options.text: Each House of Congress
The state legislature
options.misconception: confuses state election law with membership judgment

questions.explanation: Each House is the judge of the elections, returns, and qualifications of its own members. The courts and executive do not hold that power.
questions.hint: Each House judges its own members.

questions.learningObjective: State the quorum requirement for each House
questions.stem: A quorum graph asks how many members make a quorum; what is correct?

options.text: All members of each House
Two-thirds of each House
One-third of each House
A majority of each House

questions.explanation: A majority of each House constitutes a quorum. Two-thirds and unanimity apply to other actions, not quorum.
questions.hint: A majority is a quorum.

options.text: Pass legislation by majority vote
Compel the attendance of absent members
Adjourn for more than three days
Elect officers of the House

questions.explanation: A smaller number may adjourn from day to day and compel attendance of absent members. It may not legislate or elect officers.
questions.hint: It may compel attendance.

questions.stem: An expulsion graph asks what vote removes a member; what is required?

options.text: Three-fourths of all members
A simple majority of members present
Two-thirds of members present
A unanimous vote of the House

questions.explanation: Expulsion requires a two-thirds vote. A simple majority suffices for ordinary business, not for removing a member.
questions.hint: Two-thirds expels a member.

options.text: Punish members or others for disorderly behavior
Determine the rules of its own proceedings
Keep a Journal of proceedings
Arrest non-members except for treason, felony, or breach of the peace

questions.explanation: Each House may punish members and determine its rules, but may arrest non-members only for treason, felony, or breach of the peace. The other items are permitted or required.

Each House keeps a Journal and publishes it, except parts requiring secrecy
No Journal is required
The Journal is published only after the session ends

Congress may not adjourn for more than three days total

options.misconception: assigns the limit to the President

The Supreme Court must approve adjournments over three days

At all times while in office
During attendance at sessions and in going to and returning from them
Only when the member is on committee business

Only offices requiring Senate confirmation

questions.topic: Why the text has no pocket veto
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the text has no pocket veto
questions.stem: A student explains why the constitutional text contains no pocket veto; give a model answer.

answer.exemplar: The text provides only that a bill becomes law if the President does not return it within ten days while Congress is in session, so an unsigned bill becomes law rather than dying.

questions.explanation: The text's ten-day rule makes an unsigned bill law when Congress is in session. The pocket veto arises only when Congress is not in session to receive the return.

A secret ballot
A two-thirds vote of the Supreme Court

questions.learningObjective: Apply the House electorate rule to a state
questions.stem: A state sets House voter qualifications differently from its larger legislative house; is that valid?

options.text: Yes, Congress may set separate House qualifications
No, House qualifications must match the larger house's electorate
Yes, states have unlimited power over House qualifications
No, only property owners may vote for the House

questions.explanation: Article One ties House voter qualifications to the state's larger legislative house electorate. States may not set a different standard.
questions.hint: House qualifications follow the larger house.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The three qualifications for a Representative
questions.learningObjective: Apply Representative qualifications to a candidate
questions.stem: A twenty-four-year-old citizen of eight years seeks a House seat; is she eligible?

options.text: Yes, because eight years of citizenship suffices
Yes, because she is a long-term citizen
No, she must be at least twenty-five
No, she must have ten years of citizenship

questions.explanation: A Representative must be at least twenty-five. Eight years of citizenship meets that requirement, but the age floor is not met.
questions.hint: Age twenty-five is required.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The gap between the two sets of qualifications
questions.learningObjective: Compare two candidates' qualifications
questions.stem: A thirty-year-old citizen of eight years seeks either chamber; for which is she eligible?

options.text: Neither chamber
Senate only
Both chambers
options.misconception: ignores that the Senate needs nine years

options.text: House only

questions.explanation: Eight years of citizenship and age thirty satisfy the House requirements but not the Senate's nine-year citizenship requirement. She is eligible for the House only.
questions.hint: Senate requires nine years of citizenship.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The phrase that differs between the two houses
questions.learningObjective: Apply the differing phrase to a timing question
questions.stem: A senator must be thirty when elected; does the House require its members to be twenty-five when elected?

options.text: Yes, both chambers use when elected
options.misconception: reads the Senate's phrase into the House clause

options.text: No, the House requires age twenty-five at birth
No, the House clause lacks the when elected phrase
Yes, but only for first-term members

questions.explanation: The when elected phrase appears only in the Senate clause. The House clause sets age twenty-five without that timing qualifier.
questions.hint: Only the Senate clause says when elected.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The people counted in the original apportionment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the original count to a population
questions.stem: A state has 5000 free persons and 1000 other persons; how many are counted for original apportionment?
questions.explanation: Free persons count fully, and three-fifths of 1000 is 600, for a total of 5600. Counting all 6000 would ignore the three-fifths rule.
questions.hint: Add free persons to three-fifths of others.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The three-fifths count worked out
questions.learningObjective: Compute three-fifths for a larger population
questions.stem: A table shows 25000 other persons; how many are added under the original three-fifths rule?
questions.explanation: Three-fifths of 25000 is 15000. Using the full count or one-fifth would be wrong.
questions.hint: Multiply by three-fifths.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The ratio that caps a state's representation
questions.learningObjective: Apply the cap ratio to a population
questions.stem: A state has 90000 persons; under the original cap of one Representative per 30000, what is the maximum number of Representatives?
questions.explanation: 90000 divided by 30000 is 3. A higher count would exceed the cap.
questions.hint: Divide population by 30000.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The original allotment of seats to thirteen states
questions.learningObjective: Apply the original allotment to a scenario
questions.stem: A new state joins before the first enumeration; does it receive a share of the original sixty-five seats?

options.text: No, because only original states may have Representatives
Yes, every state gets at least one
options.misconception: confuses the general rule with the original allotment

options.text: Yes, by popular vote
No, the sixty-five seats were fixed among the thirteen states

questions.explanation: The original allotment of sixty-five seats was fixed among the thirteen states until the first enumeration. New states were not part of that allotment.
questions.hint: The sixty-five seats were fixed for thirteen states.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How often the enumeration must be taken
questions.learningObjective: Apply the enumeration interval to a schedule
questions.stem: An enumeration is taken in 1790; in what year must the next one be taken?
questions.explanation: The interval is ten years, so 1790 plus ten is 1800. A five- or twenty-year interval would be wrong.
questions.hint: Add ten years.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who issues a writ for a House vacancy
questions.learningObjective: Apply the writ rule to a vacancy
questions.stem: A House seat becomes vacant; who must issue the writ of election?

options.text: The President
options.misconception: assigns the duty to the executive branch

options.text: The Speaker of the House
options.misconception: confuses House authority with state authority

options.text: The governor of the state
The chief judge of the state
options.misconception: assigns the duty to the judiciary

questions.explanation: The executive authority of the state issues the writ. The Speaker, President, and judiciary do not.
questions.hint: The governor issues the writ.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The one vote each senator has
questions.learningObjective: Apply the senatorial vote rule to a roll call
questions.stem: A state has two senators; how many votes do they cast together on a bill?

options.text: Four votes, two per senator
One vote shared between them
A vote weighted by state population
Two votes

questions.explanation: Each senator has one vote, so two senators cast two votes. Weighted or shared votes are not allowed.
questions.hint: One vote per senator.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Dividing the Senate into three classes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the three-class rule to election timing
questions.stem: The Senate has 100 members in three classes; roughly how many face election in a given two-year cycle?
questions.explanation: One-third of 100 is about 33. The classes are roughly equal, so about one-third faces election each cycle.
questions.hint: About one-third is elected each cycle.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The temporary appointment sentence in Section 3
questions.learningObjective: Apply the temporary appointment rule to a vacancy
questions.stem: A senator dies; may the governor appoint a replacement until the next election?

options.text: No, no appointment is ever allowed
Yes, if the state legislature has provided for it
Yes, unconditionally for the full term
No, only the Senate may fill the seat
options.misconception: confuses vacancy with internal Senate business

questions.explanation: The executive may make temporary appointments until the next election, as the state legislature provides. Unconditional full-term appointment is not authorized.
questions.hint: Temporary appointment depends on state law.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The Vice President as President of the Senate
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Vice President's tie-breaking vote
questions.stem: The Senate is tied 50-50; may the Vice President cast a vote to break the tie?

options.text: Yes, the Vice President votes on every bill
No, the Vice President never votes
Yes, the Vice President votes only to break ties
No, only the President pro tempore breaks ties
options.misconception: assigns the power to the wrong officer

questions.explanation: The Vice President votes only to break ties. Routine voting power belongs to senators.
questions.hint: The Vice President breaks ties only.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two occasions for a President pro tempore
questions.learningObjective: Apply the President pro tempore rule to a scenario
questions.stem: The Vice President is absent from the chamber; who presides?

options.text: No one, the Senate cannot meet
options.misconception: understates the Senate's ability to preside

options.text: The Speaker of the House
The Chief Justice
The President pro tempore

questions.explanation: When the Vice President is absent, the President pro tempore presides. The Senate can still meet and conduct business.
questions.hint: The President pro tempore presides in the Vice President's absence.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who presides over a presidential trial
questions.learningObjective: Apply the presiding rule to a presidential impeachment
questions.stem: The President is impeached and tried in the Senate; who presides?

options.text: The Vice President
options.misconception: the Vice President presides over non-presidential trials

options.text: The Chief Justice
The President pro tempore
The Speaker of the House

questions.explanation: The Chief Justice presides over a presidential impeachment trial. The Vice President and President pro tempore preside over other trials.
questions.hint: The Chief Justice presides.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two-thirds that convicts
questions.learningObjective: Apply the conviction threshold to a vote count
questions.stem: Sixty senators are present at an impeachment trial; what is the minimum number needed to convict?
questions.explanation: Two-thirds of 60 is 40. A lower number would not reach the conviction threshold.
questions.hint: Two-thirds of members present.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What a judgment on impeachment may reach
questions.learningObjective: Apply the judgment scope to a sanction
questions.stem: The Senate convicts an officer; may it also impose a prison sentence?

options.text: Yes, if the President approves
Yes, imprisonment is permitted
No, judgment may only remove and disqualify
No, judgment may only censure

questions.explanation: An impeachment judgment may remove and disqualify. Criminal penalties are left to ordinary courts, so imprisonment is not available.
questions.hint: Only removal and disqualification.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The three things the Elections Clause names
questions.learningObjective: Apply the Elections Clause to a state law
questions.stem: A state law sets polling hours and ballot design; does the Elections Clause cover those?

options.text: Yes, but only for federal elections
No, states have no authority over polling hours
options.misconception: denies state authority the clause grants

options.text: No, only Congress may set polling hours
Yes, as part of manner and places

questions.explanation: Polling hours and ballot design fall within times, places, and manner. The state default applies, subject to congressional override.
questions.hint: Times, places, and manner include those details.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The one thing Congress may not alter about elections
questions.learningObjective: Apply the non-alterable limit to a bill
questions.stem: Congress passes a law changing the date of senatorial elections; is that valid?

options.text: Yes, Congress may alter any election time
No, Congress may not alter the times of choosing Senators
Yes, but only with state consent
No, because states control all election dates

questions.explanation: The Elections Clause protects the times of choosing Senators from congressional alteration. Congress may alter other election times.
questions.hint: Senatorial election times are protected.
